Browser basics::Browser contexts.summary: Browser contexts are isolated, incognito-like sessions for Playwright tests and scenarios. Use a fresh context to keep cookies, storage, permissions, and other browser state separate.
Browser basics::Browser contexts.explanation: A browser context is an independent, incognito-like session created inside a browser. It separates pages from other contexts, including their cookies, local storage, session storage, and permissions; contexts can also model different users or device settings within one browser process.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Options used to configure the new isolated browser context, such as permissions, locale, or color scheme.

example.title: Create and close an isolated context
example.explanation: Creates an isolated context, opens a page within it, then closes the context and browser.

useCases.title: Test isolation
useCases.scenario: Run each test with independent browser state so cookies or storage from one test cannot affect another.

useCases.title: Multi-user workflows
useCases.scenario: Open separate contexts for two users and exercise their interaction in one scenario.

useCases.title: Environment emulation
useCases.scenario: Configure separate device, permission, locale, or color-scheme environments.

interview.question: What is a browser context?
interview.answer: A browser context is an isolated browser session. It has independent cookies, local storage, session storage, and other browser state, while multiple contexts can run in one browser.
interview.followUp: How would you test two users in one scenario? Create two contexts, create a page in each, and use them as separate sessions.

interview.question: How does Playwright use contexts for test isolation?
interview.answer: The Playwright test runner creates a fresh context for each test by default. When using Playwright directly, create one with browser.newContext(), then create pages from that context.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful? Independent state prevents one test or user session from contaminating another.

interview.question: How do you create and clean up a context?
interview.answer: Use browser.newContext() to create the context and context.newPage() to create a page in it. After the scenario, call context.close(), then close the browser.
interview.followUp: Can contexts emulate different environments? Yes; the documentation lists mobile devices, permissions, locale, and color scheme as supported scenarios.

keyPoints: Each test can begin in a clean context, making its browser state independent from other tests.
Context isolation includes local storage, session storage, and cookies, not only the visible page.
Multiple isolated scenarios can share one browser process without sharing context state.
Outside the test runner, application code can explicitly create contexts with browser.newContext().
Context options support scenarios involving device characteristics, permissions, locale, and color scheme.
One scenario can contain several contexts, which is useful for modeling concurrent independent sessions.

Browser basics::Downloads and uploads.summary: Capture browser downloads by waiting for the download event before triggering the action, then inspect the Download object or save the file to a chosen path. Playwright also supports configuring a downloads directory at browser launch.
Browser basics::Downloads and uploads.explanation: Playwright emits a download event when an attachment starts downloading. Begin waiting before the action that triggers it, then use the Download object to inspect metadata or save the completed file; temporary files are removed when their browser context closes.
Browser basics::Downloads and uploads.returns: A Download object from the download event; saveAs copies it to a user-specified path, while path returns the completed temporary file path.

example.title: Capture and persist a download
example.explanation: Wait for the download before triggering it, save it to a test-owned path, and assert its resulting URL.

useCases.title: Validate generated downloads
useCases.scenario: A test must verify that clicking an export control produces the expected artifact.

useCases.title: Persist files for later assertions
useCases.scenario: A test suite needs downloadable artifacts retained after a browser context closes.

useCases.title: Monitor arbitrary downloads
useCases.scenario: A test needs to log or inspect downloads initiated by unpredictable page actions.

interview.question: How do you reliably capture a download?
interview.answer: Register page.waitForEvent('download') before clicking the control that starts the download. Await the promise, then call saveAs with a destination path; this preserves the file beyond the context lifetime.
interview.followUp: What if the initiating action is unknown? Attach a page.on('download') handler and inspect or process each Download object as it arrives.

interview.question: What information can a Download provide?
interview.answer: A Download exposes the downloaded URL, suggested filename, and payload-related access through the object. Its path becomes available after completion, while saveAs can safely be called during the transfer and waits if necessary.
interview.followUp: How would you handle a canceled download? Treat path access as fallible because the API reports an error for failed or canceled downloads, and assert the expected outcome.

interview.question: How can download storage be configured?
interview.answer: The browser launch option downloadsPath can choose where downloaded files are persisted. In Playwright Test, accepted downloads are enabled by default through acceptDownloads unless configured otherwise.
interview.followUp: Why still call saveAs when downloadsPath is configured? Use saveAs for an explicit, test-controlled destination and clearer artifact ownership.

keyPoints: Listen for the download event to observe every attachment initiated by the page.
The Download object provides the URL, suggested filename, and access to the downloaded payload.
Set downloadsPath at browser launch when a configured persistence location is preferable.
gotchas: Persist downloads with saveAs when the test needs files after the browser context ends.
Create the download wait before the triggering action so the event cannot be missed.

Browser basics::Network interception.summary: Playwright network routing lets tests observe, forward, mock, modify, or fail matching HTTP and HTTPS requests. Use it to make loading behavior deterministic and to exercise error states without depending on live services.
Browser basics::Network interception.explanation: Playwright places routes between the page and the browser network stack. A matching handler can inspect the request, continue it to the server, fulfill it directly with a chosen response, or abort it to simulate failure; routes can be attached to a page or an entire browser context.

parameters.name: url
parameters.description: URL pattern used to select requests for interception.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Callback invoked with the matching Route object.

Browser basics::Network interception.returns: A configured route; matching requests are handled by the supplied callback.

example.title: Fulfill a request with test data
example.explanation: Register a route before navigation so matching requests receive a deterministic mocked response.

useCases.title: Mock successful responses
useCases.scenario: Return stable API data without contacting a backend.

useCases.title: Test failure handling
useCases.scenario: Return an error or terminate a request deliberately.

useCases.title: Observe and modify traffic
useCases.scenario: Inspect or alter requests while retaining real network behavior.

useCases.title: Control context-wide traffic
useCases.scenario: Apply the same interception policy to multiple pages.

interview.question: How can network requests be intercepted in Playwright?
interview.answer: Use `page.route()` for one page or `browserContext.route()` to cover every page in a context. The route handler can inspect the request and choose how to handle it.
interview.followUp: How would you mock an endpoint for popup pages? Register the route on the browser context, because context routing applies across pages in that context.

interview.question: How do you mock an API response?
interview.answer: Call `route.fulfill()` to return a response without contacting the network. Provide options such as status, content type, and body to control the deterministic result.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the real response while changing it? Fetch the original response through the request API and pass that response to `route.fulfill()` with overrides.

interview.question: What are the main actions available inside a route handler?
interview.answer: Call `route.continue()` to send the request onward, `route.fulfill()` to answer it locally, or `route.abort()` to fail it. These choices let tests cover success, modified, and network-failure states.
interview.followUp: What happens if a matching handler does none of these? The request stalls until it is handled, so the handler must complete one of those actions.

keyPoints: Network interception supports observing and changing both HTTP and HTTPS traffic.
Page-generated XHR and fetch traffic can be monitored, modified, or handled by routes.
Choose page routing for local scope or context routing for all pages in the context.
A route handler runs at the boundary between page activity and the browser network stack.
Continue forwards the request, fulfill supplies a local response, and abort simulates a failed request.
gotchas: A fulfilled redirect is not re-intercepted, so do not rely on a second route handler for the redirect.

Browser basics::Pages and popups.summary: Playwright models each tab or popup as a Page inside a BrowserContext. Listen at context scope for any new page, or wait for an opener-specific popup before triggering the action to avoid races.
Browser basics::Pages and popups.explanation: A BrowserContext can contain multiple Page objects, representing tabs or popup windows. Subscribe to the context's page event when any newly created page matters; for a popup tied to one page, wait for that page's popup event before triggering the action, then await the resulting Page and interact with it normally.
Browser basics::Pages and popups.returns: The popup-waiting pattern resolves to the newly opened Page; the context page event supplies a newly created Page, which may still be loading.

example.title: Wait for and use a popup
example.explanation: Register the popup wait before the action that opens it, then use the returned Page like any other page.

useCases.title: Handle target=_blank navigation
useCases.scenario: A test clicks a link that opens a new tab and must verify the destination.

useCases.title: Interact with an opener-specific popup
useCases.scenario: A workflow opens a child window whose controls must be exercised after creation.

useCases.title: Monitor all context pages
useCases.scenario: A test suite must observe pages created by any action in one isolated context.

interview.question: What does a Playwright Page represent, and how are new pages detected?
interview.answer: A Page represents one tab or popup in a BrowserContext, and a context may contain multiple pages. Use the context page event to observe every newly created page, including popups.
interview.followUp: How do you limit handling to a popup opened by one page? Listen for that page's popup event or wait for it with page.waitForEvent('popup').

interview.question: How do you avoid a race condition when a click opens a popup?
interview.answer: Create the wait before the action: call page.waitForEvent('popup'), trigger the click, then await the promise. The resulting Page can be navigated and queried normally.
interview.followUp: Why must the wait be created first? The popup event may be emitted during the click, so registering afterward can miss it and race with the action.

interview.question: When should you use the context page event instead of the page popup event?
interview.answer: Use browserContext.on('page') when all new pages in the context are relevant. Use page.on('popup') or page.waitForEvent('popup') when only popups associated with a particular opener matter.
interview.followUp: What loading concern remains with the context event? The Page can arrive while still loading, so wait for an appropriate load state before inspecting it.

keyPoints: Treat a browser context as a container for several tabs or popup windows, each represented by its own Page object.
Use the Page API for navigation and content interaction regardless of whether the underlying browser surface is a tab or popup.
Subscribe at BrowserContext scope when the test must discover pages created anywhere in that context.
Context-level page handling covers pages opened by links that target a new browsing surface.
For an opener-specific workflow, obtain the child Page from the initiating page's popup event.
After resolving the popup, use ordinary locators, assertions, navigation, and other Page operations on it.
gotchas: Begin waiting for the popup before performing the click that opens it; otherwise the event can be missed.
A page popup listener is specific to the owning page, but the same popup also produces the broader BrowserContext page event.

Configuration::Playwright Test configura.summary: Playwright Test configuration centralizes run-wide defaults and project-specific variants. Configure browsers and devices, reporters, time limits, and development servers in one playwright.config.ts file.
Configuration::Playwright Test configura.explanation: Playwright reads a configuration object exported from playwright.config.ts. Global options establish defaults such as test timeouts and reporters, while projects define separate browser or environment variants. The webServer entry starts a local application before tests and can reuse an existing server outside CI.

parameters.name: timeout
parameters.description: Maximum duration of one test in milliseconds; defaults to 30 seconds.

parameters.name: globalTimeout
parameters.description: Maximum duration of the whole test run in milliseconds; zero disables the limit.

parameters.name: reporter
parameters.description: Reporter configuration for test results.

parameters.name: projects
parameters.description: Array of browser, device, or environment configurations.

parameters.name: webServer
parameters.description: Configuration for launching and waiting for a development server.

Configuration::Playwright Test configura.returns: A Playwright Test configuration object consumed by the test runner.

example.explanation: This config runs tests with a shared timeout, HTML reporting, two browser projects, and a local server that starts before testing.

useCases.scenario: Responsive UI testing

useCases.scenario: Local application testing
