interview.question: Why use Playwright projects?
interview.answer: Projects let one configuration run tests in multiple configurations, such as different browsers or devices. Put project-specific settings in projects, while top-level options provide shared defaults.
interview.followUp: How would you target only one configured browser? Use the CLI project selector with that project's name, for example `--project=chromium`.

interview.question: How do timeout and globalTimeout differ?
interview.answer: timeout limits each test and defaults to 30 seconds; time spent in the test function, fixtures, and beforeEach hooks counts toward it. globalTimeout instead limits the complete test run and is unlimited by default.
interview.followUp: Why set globalTimeout in CI? It bounds hanging runs while allowing Playwright to stop the run and let reporters produce a report.

interview.question: How does webServer prepare an application for tests?
interview.answer: webServer launches a development server before tests. Configure its command and either its URL or port; reuseExistingServer can avoid starting another instance when an appropriate server already exists.
interview.followUp: What if startup is slow? Increase webServer.timeout, whose default is 60,000 milliseconds.

keyPoints: Export the Playwright Test configuration from the project config file to centralize test-run settings.
Use projects to execute the same suite against separate browser or device profiles.
Set reporter to choose how test execution results are presented, including built-in or custom reporters.
Projects can represent browser, device, environment, timeout, or retry variations.
Use webServer to start a local development server before Playwright begins the test run.
globalTimeout caps the entire run and preserves reporter output when the limit is reached.
gotchas: The test timeout includes the test body, fixtures, and beforeEach hooks; increase or override it when setup work is slow.
A web server definition must identify either the expected URL or the port Playwright should wait for.

Configuration::Projects and browsers.summary: Playwright projects let one test suite run under multiple browser, device, environment, or authentication configurations. Define named projects in `playwright.config.ts`, then run all projects or select specific ones with `--project`.
Configuration::Projects and browsers.explanation: A Playwright project is a named group of tests sharing configuration. Add projects to `playwright.config.ts`, give each a browser or device setup, and Playwright can execute the same suite for every configured variant; projects can also target separate environments or authentication states.

parameters.name: projects
parameters.description: Named project definitions, each containing shared test settings and optional browser or device configuration.

parameters.name: use
parameters.description: Project-specific browser, device, and test-use settings.

Configuration::Projects and browsers.returns: Runs tests for the configured projects; selecting `--project` limits execution to the named project.

example.title: Configure browser projects
example.explanation: Define browser and device variants as projects, then run the suite with `npx playwright test` or select one with `--project`.

useCases.title: Run the suite on Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.
useCases.scenario: Browser compatibility

useCases.title: Reuse tests with emulated desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.
useCases.scenario: Responsive behavior

useCases.title: Run equivalent tests against staging and production configurations.
useCases.scenario: Deployment validation

useCases.title: Exercise the suite with separate authenticated project states.
useCases.scenario: Authentication variants

interview.question: What is a Playwright project and why use one?
interview.answer: A project is a logical group of tests with the same configuration. Define projects in `playwright.config.ts`; each can specify a browser, device, or other test settings, and the suite runs across them.
interview.followUp: How would you execute only Firefox? Use the project name with `npx playwright test --project firefox`.

interview.question: How do you configure the same tests for multiple browsers?
interview.answer: Put browser variants in the `projects` array and configure each project's `use` settings, commonly by spreading a device descriptor. Running `npx playwright test` then executes the configured suite for all projects.
interview.followUp: How can you run two selected variants? Pass `--project` once for each name, such as `--project webkit --project firefox`.

interview.question: What other configurations can projects represent?
interview.answer: Projects are not limited to browser choice. They can separate environments such as staging and production, apply different timeouts or retries, split tests by package or functionality, and represent other configurations.
interview.followUp: What is the command-line mechanism for narrowing the run? Repeat the `--project` option for every desired project.

keyPoints: Each project names a group of tests that shares one configuration.
Projects let one suite cover different browser engines and device profiles.
Declare the project matrix in the Playwright configuration file.
The same test files can be evaluated repeatedly under different project settings.
Built-in browser-engine variants include Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox.
A project can use emulated tablet or mobile device profiles.
gotchas: Selecting a project with `--project` runs only that configured project rather than the complete matrix.
In the VS Code extension, the first configured project is selected unless other projects are chosen.

Debugging::Trace viewer.summary: Trace Viewer is Playwright’s GUI for replaying a recorded test trace. It helps diagnose failures by stepping through actions and reviewing DOM snapshots, logs, network activity, errors, console output, and source.
Debugging::Trace viewer.explanation: A trace is a recorded, time-navigable account of a test run. Trace Viewer lets you select or hover over actions, inspect the page state around them through DOM snapshots, and examine logs, source, network activity, errors, and console messages; the snapshot can also be inspected with browser DevTools.
Debugging::Trace viewer.returns: A browsable view of a saved Playwright trace; the viewer itself does not return a programmatic value.

example.title: Capture a trace for later inspection
example.explanation: Run the test with tracing enabled, then open the produced ZIP with the Playwright CLI.

useCases.title: Diagnose CI failures
useCases.scenario: A test fails in CI and an artifact contains its trace ZIP.

useCases.title: Inspect action timing and DOM state
useCases.scenario: An action behaves unexpectedly and its page state must be reconstructed.

useCases.title: Investigate network and console diagnostics
useCases.scenario: A request or browser message may explain a failure.

interview.question: What is Trace Viewer, and when is it useful?
interview.answer: Trace Viewer is a GUI for exploring a recorded Playwright trace after the test has run. It lets you move through actions and inspect the corresponding page state and diagnostic data.
interview.followUp: How can a remote trace be opened? Use the CLI with the trace URL, for example `npx playwright show-trace https://example.com/trace.zip`.

interview.question: What information can be inspected for an action?
interview.answer: Select an action or use the timeline to see the page state before and after it. The viewer also exposes the action details, log, source, network, errors, and console.
interview.followUp: How can the page markup be investigated further? Use the DOM snapshot and open browser DevTools to inspect the HTML and CSS.

interview.question: How is a trace opened after a run?
interview.answer: Record a trace during test execution by enabling tracing, save it as a ZIP archive, and open that archive with `npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`. The HTML report can also provide a trace entry for a test.
interview.followUp: What is a convenient CI workflow? Preserve the trace ZIP as an artifact, then open it locally or pass its remote URL to the CLI.

keyPoints: It is a graphical interface for investigating a completed test run rather than a live browser-control API.
The timeline supports time-based navigation across individual test actions.
Per-step diagnostics include logs, source, network requests, errors, and console output.
DOM snapshots make the recorded page structure interactive for investigation.
The Actions tab shows the locator involved and the duration of each action.
gotchas: The online viewer processes the trace in the browser, but a trace must first be recorded and saved before it can be inspected.
When opening a local archive with the CLI, provide its complete path.

Debugging::Tracing and debugging.summary: Playwright tracing records browser actions and network activity into an archive for Trace Viewer. With screenshots and DOM snapshots enabled, it provides visual, page-structure, and request evidence for debugging failed tests.
Debugging::Tracing and debugging.explanation: Enable tracing for a test run, then inspect its saved trace in Trace Viewer. The viewer lets you move through actions and examine the page state, DOM snapshots, screenshots, network requests, console output, and errors to diagnose failures.
Debugging::Tracing and debugging.syntax:
await context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true });
await context.tracing.stop({ path: 'trace.zip' });

example.title: Run a test with tracing
example.explanation: Run with `npx playwright test --trace on`; then open the generated trace from the HTML report or with Trace Viewer.

useCases.title: Diagnose CI-only failures
useCases.scenario: A test fails intermittently in CI and needs evidence from the failing retry.

useCases.title: Inspect action timing and page state
useCases.scenario: A click or navigation behaves differently from expected and the failure location is unclear.

useCases.title: Investigate network behavior
useCases.scenario: A page appears correct visually but an API response or request causes the test to fail.

interview.question: What does Playwright tracing capture, and how is it used?
interview.answer: Tracing records browser operations and network activity, then saves the result for Trace Viewer. Enable screenshots and snapshots when using the tracing API to add visual and DOM evidence.
interview.followUp: What is missing from a context trace? Test assertions, including `expect` calls, are not recorded, so assertion diagnostics must come from the test framework output.

interview.question: What evidence can Trace Viewer provide during debugging?
interview.answer: Trace Viewer presents a timeline of test actions and lets you inspect the state around each action. It also exposes logs, source, network traffic, errors, console messages, screenshots, and DOM snapshots.
interview.followUp: How can the DOM be investigated further? Open the DOM snapshot and use browser DevTools to inspect its HTML and CSS.

interview.question: How should tracing be configured for failed CI tests?
interview.answer: For CI failures, configure traces with a test option such as `on-first-retry`, so a retry produces diagnostic evidence without retaining a trace for every successful run. The trace can then be opened from the HTML report.
interview.followUp: How can tracing be forced during local development? Run Playwright with `--trace on` to record traces locally.

keyPoints: Begin recording before the interactions you need to diagnose; actions performed earlier will not appear in that trace.
Finish the capture explicitly and write the trace archive so Trace Viewer can open it.
Enable screenshots to create visual timeline evidence that shows how the page appeared during actions.
Snapshots and network recording connect each action with page structure and HTTP activity.
gotchas: A trace does not include test assertions such as `expect` calls, so assertion failures need the test output or report as well.

Fixtures::Authentication state.summary: Reuse a prepared authenticated browser state so tests skip repeated login while retaining Playwright’s isolated browser contexts.
Fixtures::Authentication state.explanation: Authentication state is captured from an authenticated browser context with storageState and saved to a file. Configure the storageState option to initialize each test context with that state, while Playwright still creates isolated browser contexts for tests.

parameters.name: storageState
parameters.description: A path to saved storage state or an in-memory storage-state value used to initialize the browser context.

Fixtures::Authentication state.returns: A saved storage-state file is produced when BrowserContext.storageState() is called; the test option initializes contexts from that state.

example.title: Save and reuse authenticated state
example.explanation: A setup test saves authenticated browser state, and the configuration reuses it when creating test contexts.

useCases.title: Shared authenticated account
useCases.scenario: A suite has many tests that require the same signed-in user.

useCases.title: Per-worker authentication
useCases.scenario: Parallel execution needs independent users rather than one account shared by workers.

useCases.title: Multiple authenticated roles
useCases.scenario: The suite validates permissions for different signed-in roles.

interview.question: How do you reuse authentication across tests?
interview.answer: Use `browserContext.storageState()` to save the current authenticated context, then provide the resulting file through the `storageState` test option. New test contexts begin with the saved login information.
interview.followUp: How can parallel workers avoid sharing one account? Override the `storageState` fixture and authenticate once per worker, differentiating workers with `testInfo.parallelIndex`.

interview.question: How should a test suite prepare shared authentication state?
interview.answer: Create a setup project that authenticates once and writes the state file. Declare that project as a dependency of the projects that consume the state, so setup runs first.
interview.followUp: What should happen when the saved session expires? Delete the stored state and run authentication again to produce a fresh file.

interview.question: Why use storage state instead of logging in in every test?
interview.answer: Browser contexts provide isolation between tests, while the saved state avoids repeating the login flow. This preserves reproducibility and speeds up execution.
interview.followUp: How can different authenticated roles be tested? Configure a distinct `storageState` file, such as an administrator state, for the relevant tests.

keyPoints: Tests can start with a previously captured authenticated session instead of performing login each time.
The login routine creates a reusable state artifact on disk.
Applying the artifact makes tests begin in a signed-in condition.
Set the authenticated file as the storageState for projects that need it.
Use the worker's parallel index to create separate per-worker authentication identities.
gotchas: Keep the authentication-state directory out of version control.
Remove and regenerate the saved state when the session expires.
A setup project must run before dependent test projects when it prepares shared state.

Fixtures::Test hooks.summary: Use beforeEach and afterEach for scoped per-test setup and cleanup. When setup and teardown belong to one reusable resource, compose them as a fixture with test.extend().
Fixtures::Test hooks.explanation: Hooks run around tests in their containing file or describe group, while fixtures provide isolated, reusable setup and teardown. Prefer composing setup and cleanup into fixtures when both belong to the same resource, then request the fixture in tests or hooks through their arguments.
Fixtures::Test hooks.syntax:
test.beforeEach(hookFunction)
test.beforeEach(title, hookFunction)
test.afterEach(hookFunction)
test.afterEach(title, hookFunction)
test.extend(fixtures)

parameters.name: hookFunction
parameters.description: Callback receiving the available fixtures and optionally TestInfo; runs before each matching test.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Optional label for the hook.

Fixtures::Test hooks.returns: A test hook registration; the documentation does not specify a meaningful return value.

example.title: Per-test setup and cleanup
example.explanation: The hooks prepare the page before each test and clear browser state afterward; Playwright supplies the page fixture to both hooks and the test.

useCases.title: Scoped per-test preparation
useCases.scenario: A group of tests needs the same navigation, authentication, or test data preparation before every case.

useCases.title: Per-test cleanup
useCases.scenario: Each test creates browser state or another resource that must be removed regardless of the test outcome.

useCases.title: Composable resource lifecycle
useCases.scenario: Multiple tests or files need a reusable resource with setup and teardown managed together.

interview.question: What is the scope and input of test.beforeEach()?
interview.answer: beforeEach runs before every test in its file, or before every test in the enclosing test.describe() group. It can receive the same fixtures as the test body and an optional TestInfo object.
interview.followUp: How would you make the behavior global? Define an auto fixture whose setup runs automatically for tests, rather than relying on a file-local hook.

interview.question: How should beforeEach and afterEach be used together?
interview.answer: afterEach is intended for per-test teardown and can clean up resources created by beforeEach. Both hooks can use fixtures, so cleanup can operate on the same test-specific environment.
interview.followUp: When should cleanup move into a fixture? When setup and teardown form one reusable resource lifecycle, use a fixture with teardown after await use().

interview.question: Why use fixtures instead of paired hooks?
interview.answer: A custom fixture is created by extending the test object with test.extend(). Its setup occurs before the test or hook that requires it, and its teardown occurs after await use() when no longer needed.
interview.followUp: How does fixture composition work? A fixture can request other fixtures as arguments, allowing Playwright to build only the dependency graph needed by the test.

keyPoints: Fixtures establish the environment required by each test and keep that setup isolated.
A hook can request fixtures through its argument object, just like a test function.
A fixture owns both lifecycle phases, making resource cleanup adjacent to resource creation.
Playwright prepares a requested fixture immediately before the dependent test or hook.
Fixture cleanup waits until its dependents finish and the fixture is no longer needed.
Use an automatic fixture when per-test behavior must apply across files.
gotchas: Hooks are scoped to the file or test.describe() block where they are declared; they do not automatically apply globally.
Paired setup and cleanup hooks can be harder to reuse; model the resource as a fixture instead.
Registration order matters when several beforeEach hooks have dependencies.

Learning module::Playwright learning mod.summary: Playwright Test lets engineers write end-to-end tests as browser actions followed by assertions. Its fixtures provide isolated pages, while auto-waiting assertions and hooks support reliable, maintainable test suites.
Learning module::Playwright learning mod.explanation: Playwright Test supplies a test function, fixtures such as an isolated page, and expect-based assertions. Tests perform browser actions, while assertions wait for the expected state; hooks can prepare or clean up shared test behavior.

example.title: A basic Playwright test
example.explanation: This test navigates with the isolated page fixture and verifies the page title with an auto-waiting assertion.

useCases.title: End-to-end workflow checks
useCases.scenario: Verify a user workflow such as navigation, form submission, or visible page content.

useCases.title: Isolated browser-state testing
useCases.scenario: Run independent tests without leaking cookies, storage, or page state between cases.

useCases.title: Reusable setup and teardown
useCases.scenario: Prepare data or resources before tests and clean them up afterward.

interview.question: What are the main building blocks of a Playwright test?
interview.answer: A test declares browser behavior with `test` and checks outcomes with `expect`. The built-in `page` fixture gives the test a browser page, and assertions can wait for an expected condition.
interview.followUp: How does Playwright reduce flaky timing failures? Its actions perform actionability checks automatically, while async assertions wait until their expected condition is met.

interview.question: How does Playwright Test isolate tests?
interview.answer: Each test gets a separate Browser Context, which behaves like a new browser profile. This keeps pages and browser state isolated even when tests share one browser process.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful for parallel execution? Independent contexts prevent one test's cookies or storage from contaminating another test.

interview.question: When should you use Playwright test hooks?
interview.answer: Use hooks such as `test.beforeEach` and `test.afterEach` for work around every test. Use `test.beforeAll` and `test.afterAll` for work performed once per worker around the group's tests.
interview.followUp: When should setup be moved into a fixture? When the setup represents reusable test environment state that should be prepared and torn down according to each test's needs.

keyPoints: A test combines browser actions with assertions about the resulting state.
Use `expect` with a matcher that expresses the condition the test should verify.
Async assertion matchers retry while waiting for the expected condition.
Fixtures provide prepared resources, including the built-in `page` fixture.
Tests receive fresh environments so they can run independently.
Use `test.describe` to organize related tests into a group.
gotchas: Do not add arbitrary waits before actions; Playwright waits for actionability automatically.
Do not assume state survives between tests: each test receives an isolated browser context.
beforeAll and afterAll run once per worker, not once for every test.

Locators::Locator filtering.summary: Use locator.filter() to narrow repeated components by descendant text or a related locator. Chain the resulting locator to reach the specific control inside the matching component.
Locators::Locator filtering.explanation: Start with a locator for repeated components, then call filter() to retain only elements matching text or containing a matching descendant locator. Because filtering is relative to the original locator, chaining another role-based locator can target an action inside the narrowed component.

parameters.name: hasText
parameters.description: Text or a regular expression used to match content in the element or its descendants.

parameters.name: has
parameters.description: A locator whose match must be contained by each candidate; it must be relative to the outer locator.

Locators::Locator filtering.returns: A Locator narrowed according to the supplied filter options.

example.title: Filter a repeated list item
example.explanation: This test first narrows list items by their descendant text, then finds and clicks the button within the matching item.

useCases.title: Select one repeated component by its text
useCases.scenario: A page renders many cards, rows, or list items with the same structure.

useCases.title: Select by a descendant locator
useCases.scenario: The identifying property is a child control such as a button or checkbox.

useCases.title: Compose multiple filters
useCases.scenario: A component needs several independent constraints.

interview.question: How do you target one item in a repeated component list?
interview.answer: Use locator.filter() after locating the repeated component, for example getByRole('listitem').filter({ hasText: 'Product 2' }). It narrows the existing locator and can be chained with another locator to reach a control inside the match.
interview.followUp: How would you select by a descendant control instead of text? Use filter({ has: page.getByRole(...) }), ensuring that the has locator is relative to each outer match.

interview.question: How does filtering with a related locator work?
interview.answer: The has option keeps outer elements that contain elements matching the supplied relative locator. The inner locator is evaluated from each outer match rather than from the document root.
interview.followUp: What common mistake breaks this filter? Passing an inner locator that requires an element outside the outer locator; the relationship must be expressed within the outer component.

interview.question: What are the matching semantics of hasText?
interview.answer: A string supplied to hasText matches text somewhere inside the element, including descendants, with case-insensitive substring matching. A regular expression can be supplied when pattern-based matching is preferable.
interview.followUp: How can filtering become more precise? Combine a suitable structural or role locator with a regular expression that encodes the intended text pattern.

keyPoints: filter() refines an existing locator rather than starting a new page-wide search.
Multiple filters can be chained to express several conditions on the same repeated component.
hasText checks text in the component’s own content and descendants.
Use text-based filtering or a related locator depending on which property identifies the desired component.
After filtering, chain a role or other locator to target the required descendant action.
gotchas: A has locator is evaluated inside each outer match; do not provide a locator that depends on elements outside the original component.
A string hasText filter is not an exact, case-sensitive comparison; use a regular expression when you need stricter matching.

Locators::Role and text locators.summary: Prefer `page.getByRole()` for accessible, user-facing semantics and `page.getByText()` for visible text. Add an accessible name to role locators when possible, and use text locators mainly for non-interactive content.
Locators::Role and text locators.explanation: Role locators find elements as users and assistive technologies perceive them, using explicit or implicit accessibility information; adding an accessible name makes the match more precise. Text locators search an element’s contained text and support substring, exact, or regular-expression matching. Use roles for interactive controls and text for non-interactive content.

parameters.name: role
parameters.description: The ARIA role to locate, optionally accompanied by role-specific options such as accessible name.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text, exactness, or regular-expression criteria used to find contained text.

Locators::Role and text locators.returns: A Locator representing the matching element or elements.

example.title: Role and text locators
example.explanation: The test identifies the heading through its accessible role and name, then finds the link by its visible text.

useCases.title: Interact with accessible controls
useCases.scenario: A test needs to click a button, check a checkbox, or activate a link using the control’s accessible semantics.

useCases.title: Find visible content
useCases.scenario: A test needs to assert or locate headings, paragraphs, labels, or other non-interactive page content.

useCases.title: Reduce selector brittleness
useCases.scenario: A locator should remain aligned with user-visible behavior instead of depending on implementation-specific CSS structure.

interview.question: What does a role locator represent, and how can you make it precise?
interview.answer: Use `page.getByRole()` when the target has a meaningful accessibility role, such as a button or checkbox. It reflects how users and assistive technology perceive the page, and an accessible name can narrow the match.
interview.followUp: How would you locate a uniquely named button? Use `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' })`, then assert or interact with that locator.

interview.question: When should you use a text locator?
interview.answer: Use `page.getByText()` to find an element by text content. It supports substring matching by default and can also use exact text or a regular expression.
interview.followUp: When would text be a weaker choice? For an interactive element such as a link, button, or input, use its role locator instead.

interview.question: How do role and text locators differ in recommended usage?
interview.answer: Role locators are recommended for interactive elements because they model the semantic control exposed to users and assistive technology. Text locators are recommended for non-interactive elements such as `div`, `span`, and `p`.
interview.followUp: What should replace brittle CSS tied to implementation details? Prefer user-visible locators such as accessible roles or text.

keyPoints: `page.getByRole()` uses explicit or implicit accessibility attributes to identify elements.
Role locators model the page’s user-facing accessibility semantics rather than its DOM structure.
`page.getByText()` locates an element based on text contained within it.
Text matching can be configured as substring, exact-string, or regular-expression matching.
Use text locators for non-interactive content such as `div`, `span`, and `p` elements.
gotchas: A role alone may match more than one element, so include the accessible name whenever possible.
Do not use text matching as the primary locator for interactive controls; prefer their semantic role.

Projects and browsers::Parallel workers.summary: Playwright Test uses independent worker processes to run tests concurrently. Configure parallelism, constrain workers for shared resources, and isolate backend data to prevent races.
Projects and browsers::Parallel workers.explanation: Playwright Test starts independent OS worker processes, each with its own browser and isolated BrowserContext. Configure file-level or project-wide parallelism, limit worker count when shared resources cannot handle concurrency, and prevent data races by giving tests unique backend data or protecting shared access with named locks.

example.title: Parallel tests with isolated data
example.explanation: This runs tests in the file in separate workers and derives a distinct record identifier for each test.

useCases.title: Speed up independent test suites
useCases.scenario: A suite contains many independent tests spread across files.

useCases.title: Serialize access with named locks
useCases.scenario: Several tests need the same external service or account that rejects concurrent access.

useCases.title: Prevent backend data collisions
useCases.scenario: Concurrent tests create or modify server-side records.

useCases.title: Enable project-wide parallel execution
useCases.scenario: A project needs broader concurrency than file-level parallelism provides.

interview.question: How does Playwright execute tests across workers?
interview.answer: Playwright runs tests in independent OS worker processes, and each worker starts its own browser. By default, test files run in parallel while tests within a file run in order.
interview.followUp: How would you parallelize tests within one file? Use test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' }); each test then runs in its own worker and cannot share state.

interview.question: How can parallelism be configured?
interview.answer: Use test.describe.configure({ mode: 'parallel' }) for tests in one file. For broader scope, enable testProject.fullyParallel or testConfig.fullyParallel to run all tests in all files concurrently.
interview.followUp: What must change when tests use shared backend data? Give each test unique data, commonly by deriving an identifier from testInfo.testId.

interview.question: How should a suite handle a resource that cannot be accessed concurrently?
interview.answer: Named locks serialize only tests that use the same lock name, while unrelated tests continue running in parallel. Locks work across files, worker processes, and projects.
interview.followUp: When is lowering worker count preferable? Use fewer workers when a project shares a resource such as one account that cannot support simultaneous access.

keyPoints: Parallel execution is built into Playwright Test.
The runner scales execution by starting multiple workers concurrently.
Every worker receives the same environment but owns a separate browser instance.
In file-level parallel mode, each parallel test gets its own relevant hooks rather than sharing file-level hook state.
Named locks coordinate tests that contend for a resource without stopping unrelated parallel work.
Use testInfo.testId-derived identifiers to keep backend records distinct across concurrent tests.
gotchas: Workers are independent processes, so do not rely on communication or shared in-memory state between them.
Tests in parallel cannot safely share globals or state; put setup and data isolation at the test or worker level.
Protect non-concurrent external services or account settings with a named lock, or reduce the worker count.
Avoid reusing backend records across parallel tests; derive unique identifiers instead.

Projects and browsers::Retries and shard.summary: Use retries to re-run failed tests and expose flaky behavior, then shard the suite across CI jobs to reduce runtime. Enable fullyParallel for more even distribution across shards.
Projects and browsers::Retries and shard.explanation: Configure limited retries to identify intermittent failures as flaky while preserving genuine failures, then split the suite across CI jobs with one-based shard coordinates. Enabling fullyParallel helps distribute individual tests more evenly between shards.
Projects and browsers::Retries and shard.syntax: retries: number; shard: { total: number, current: number }; npx playwright test --shard=x/y

parameters.name: retries
parameters.description: Maximum number of retry attempts for each failed test.

parameters.name: fullyParallel
parameters.description: Whether to run individual tests in parallel across shards for even distribution.

parameters.name: shard
parameters.description: Shard index and total shard count; the index is one-based.

Projects and browsers::Retries and shard.returns: Tests are categorized as passed, flaky, or failed; the selected shard runs the tests assigned to it.

example.title: Retry failures and run one shard
example.explanation: This configuration retries failures only in CI and enables balanced distribution when the suite is split across four CI jobs.

useCases.title: Detect flaky tests
useCases.scenario: CI runs where intermittent infrastructure or timing issues can occur.

useCases.title: Speed up CI with sharding
useCases.scenario: Large suites that exceed a single CI job's practical runtime.

useCases.title: Scale browser coverage
useCases.scenario: Cross-browser pipelines with enough CI workers to run jobs concurrently.

keyPoints: Retries rerun failed tests automatically, which helps distinguish intermittent flakiness from persistent failures.
Results are classified as passed, flaky, or failed, making transient evidence visible without hiding real failures.
A test that succeeds only after retry is reported as flaky.
gotchas: Without setting retries, a failed test is not rerun.
A failure causes the worker and its browser to be discarded before testing continues in a new worker.

Test design::Assertions.summary: Use web-first assertions to verify browser state. They automatically retry until the expected condition is observed or the assertion timeout expires.
Test design::Assertions.explanation: Web-first assertions evaluate the current browser state through a locator or page object and retry the check while the application changes. The assertion passes as soon as the expected condition is observed; otherwise it fails when its timeout is reached. Assertion timeouts can be customized per assertion or globally.
Test design::Assertions.returns: Assertions pass when the expected condition is met; otherwise they fail when the assertion timeout is reached.

example.title: Retry a status assertion
example.explanation: The locator assertion rechecks the element until its text matches or the assertion timeout expires.

useCases.title: Verify eventual text
useCases.scenario: A click triggers an asynchronous UI update, and the test must verify the resulting message.

useCases.title: Check eventual visibility
useCases.scenario: An element becomes available or visible after navigation or background work.

useCases.title: Wait on browser state
useCases.scenario: A response or page property must reach an expected state without fixed sleeps.

interview.question: Why use web-first assertions for dynamic pages?
interview.answer: Web-first assertions retry the expected condition until it passes or the assertion timeout is reached. This makes them suitable for dynamic pages where the result may appear after an action.
interview.followUp: What happens during a retry? The target is fetched again and checked against the expectation, allowing the assertion to observe a later browser state.

interview.question: How do you assert that an element eventually has specific text?
interview.answer: Use a locator-based assertion such as `await expect(locator).toHaveText('Submitted')`. Playwright repeatedly evaluates the locator and its text rather than checking only once.
interview.followUp: How can the waiting period be changed? Supply an assertion timeout option for one assertion or configure the default assertion timeout globally.

interview.question: What is the default assertion timeout?
interview.answer: The default assertion timeout is five seconds. If the expected state is not observed before that limit, the assertion fails.
interview.followUp: Does increasing the timeout guarantee correctness? No; it only permits more time for the condition, while the expectation still has to become true.

keyPoints: Web-first assertions provide purpose-built methods for checking browser state.
The assertion waits and retries instead of requiring a manually inserted sleep.
A locator target is tested again during the retry cycle.
Text assertions continue until the fetched node contains the expected text.
A timeout may be supplied as an option when an individual assertion needs different timing.

Test design::Visual comparisons.summary: Playwright visual comparisons capture a page or element screenshot and compare it with a stored reference. The first run creates the baseline; later runs report visual diffs, with configurable tolerances for pixel and color differences.
Test design::Visual comparisons.explanation: Use Playwright Test's screenshot assertion to capture a page or locator and compare it with a stored reference image. The initial run establishes the baseline, while subsequent runs detect visual changes and report diffs. Tune accepted variation with options such as threshold or maxDiffPixels, and deliberately regenerate baselines with the update-snapshots flag when the UI change is expected.

parameters.name: nameOrOptions
parameters.description: Optional snapshot name, screenshot options, and assertion configuration; the page documents these under the method's options.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Additional screenshot/assertion options such as threshold and maxDiffPixels.

Test design::Visual comparisons.returns: A Playwright Test screenshot assertion that passes when the captured screenshot matches the stored reference within the configured tolerances.

example.title: Compare a page screenshot
example.explanation: The first run creates the reference image; later runs compare the current page against it.

useCases.title: Full-page visual regression
useCases.scenario: Detect unintended CSS, layout, or rendering changes on a full page during regression tests.

useCases.title: Focused region checks
useCases.scenario: Lock a critical component or region without making unrelated page changes part of the baseline.

useCases.title: Baseline maintenance
useCases.scenario: Approve an intentional UI redesign by regenerating reference images with the documented update flag.

interview.question: How does Playwright perform a visual comparison?
interview.answer: Use `expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()` to compare the current page with a stored reference. The first execution creates the reference screenshot, and later executions compare against it.
interview.followUp: How would you refresh an intentionally changed baseline? Run the test with `--update-snapshots` and review the replacement image.

interview.question: What controls can reduce false positives?
interview.answer: `threshold` controls the permitted perceived color difference for corresponding pixels, from strict `0` to lax `1`, with a default of `0.2`. `maxDiffPixels` limits how many pixels may differ.
interview.followUp: When would `maxDiffPixels` be preferable? Use it when a small, explicit number of changed pixels is acceptable regardless of the total image dimensions.

interview.question: What image formats does the documented feature support?
interview.answer: Snapshots are stored as PNG files by default. Naming the snapshot with a `.webp` extension stores it in lossless WebP format instead.
interview.followUp: How can teams organize named baselines? Supply an explicit snapshot name so the expected image is associated with a stable, meaningful identifier.

keyPoints: The feature is built into the Playwright Test runner and is intended for screenshot-based visual regression checks.
Pass a stable name to the assertion when the default snapshot naming does not express the scenario clearly.
Unspecified snapshot output uses PNG, giving baselines a predictable default format.
Threshold affects the pixel comparator's sensitivity rather than defining a maximum count of changed pixels.
Use maxDiffPixels to permit a bounded number of differing pixels in an otherwise matching screenshot.
gotchas: The first execution creates the baseline, so review that generated image before treating later comparisons as meaningful.
Update baselines explicitly when an intentional page change occurs; do not overwrite them accidentally.
A nonzero threshold allows color variation, so an overly lax value can hide real visual regressions.

Test hooks::Authentication in a setup pr.summary: Authenticate once in a Playwright setup project, save the browser state, and configure dependent projects to use it through storageState. Tests then begin authenticated without repeating a sign-in hook.
Test hooks::Authentication in a setup pr.explanation: A dedicated setup project performs authentication once and writes the resulting browser context state to an authentication file. Other projects depend on it and configure storageState to create already-authenticated contexts, avoiding repeated sign-in hooks.

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: The setup project's authentication test uses the Playwright test fixtures, especially page, to perform the sign-in flow.

parameters.name: storageState
parameters.description: The storageState option identifies the saved authentication-state file used to initialize test contexts.

Test hooks::Authentication in a setup pr.returns: The setup test produces an authentication-state file; dependent projects then create contexts populated with that state.

example.title: Authenticate in a setup project
example.explanation: The setup test signs in, saves the browser context state, and a dependent project loads that file for its tests.

useCases.title: Share one account state across tests
useCases.scenario: A suite has many tests that all require the same signed-in user.

useCases.title: Avoid repeated login work
useCases.scenario: Authentication is expensive or rate-limited.

useCases.title: Bootstrap dependent browser projects
useCases.scenario: Multiple browser projects need the same authenticated session.

useCases.title: Use worker-specific state
useCases.scenario: A test suite needs isolated authentication per parallel worker.

interview.question: How does a setup project reuse authentication?
interview.answer: A setup project is a project whose authentication test saves state, while dependent projects consume that state through storageState. The dependency ensures setup runs before the dependent tests.
interview.followUp: How would you avoid sharing one account across parallel workers? Use the documented worker-scoped fixture pattern to authenticate once per worker and provide each worker its own state.

interview.question: How is the authentication state created?
interview.answer: The setup test signs in with a page, then calls browserContext.storageState() with a file path. Playwright later uses that file to initialize test contexts with the saved authenticated state.
interview.followUp: What kinds of state can this preserve? The authentication page explains that state may involve cookies, local storage, IndexedDB, or passkeys, depending on the application.

interview.question: What security concern applies to the saved state?
interview.answer: The authentication file should be placed in playwright/.auth and ignored by version control. It may contain sensitive cookies or headers, so committing it could expose access to the application.
interview.followUp: What should happen if the state expires? Re-run the setup project to sign in again and regenerate the saved state before dependent tests run.

keyPoints: Put the sign-in flow in a setup project so the authenticated context can be reused by later tests.
Declare the setup project as a dependency of each project that needs authenticated browser contexts.
Project dependencies establish ordering: setup executes before the dependent test projects.
Setting storageState on a test project makes each newly created test context begin with the saved login state.
The sign-in routine persists the resulting browser state to a file for later context initialization.
Store authentication artifacts under playwright/.auth and exclude that directory from source control.
gotchas: Keep the authentication-state directory out of version control because it can contain sensitive session data.
A setup project is a dependency, so it runs before the dependent test projects rather than only when a particular test needs it.
Configure storageState on every project that should start authenticated; defining the setup project alone does not apply the state.

Test hooks::Automatic fixtures over hook.summary: An automatic fixture runs for each applicable test or worker without being named by the test. Put setup before await use() and teardown after it, keeping a resource’s complete lifecycle in one fixture.
Test hooks::Automatic fixtures over hook.explanation: Define setup and cleanup together in a fixture: code before await use() prepares the resource, await use() hands control to the test, and code afterward tears it down. Mark the fixture with { auto: true } when it must run for every test or worker even if the test does not request it directly.
Test hooks::Automatic fixtures over hook.syntax: fixtureName: [async ({ dependencies }, use, testInfo) => { /* setup */ await use(value); /* teardown */ }, { auto: true, scope: 'test' }]

example.title: Automatic login fixture
example.explanation: The automatic fixture logs in before each test and performs its cleanup after the test through the code following use().

useCases.title: Replace global per-test hooks
useCases.scenario: Every test needs consistent preparation and cleanup, such as authentication, tracing, or environment reset.

useCases.title: Manage worker-level resources
useCases.scenario: A resource should be initialized once for a worker and released when that worker ends.

useCases.title: Order related lifecycles
useCases.scenario: A dependent resource must be cleaned up before its prerequisite.

interview.question: How does an automatic fixture differ from an ordinary fixture?
interview.answer: Set up the resource before await use(), call await use() to provide it to the test, and put teardown afterward. This keeps lifecycle code with the fixture rather than distributing it across hooks.
interview.followUp: How do dependencies affect cleanup order? If fixture A depends on B, B starts first and is torn down after A, so dependent resources remain available during A's cleanup.

interview.question: How do you declare an automatic fixture?
interview.answer: Use tuple syntax with { auto: true }. Playwright then initializes the fixture for each applicable test or worker even when the test function does not name it.
interview.followUp: When should it be worker-scoped? Choose scope: 'worker' for setup shared by tests in a worker and cleanup only when that worker process is torn down.

interview.question: When is an automatic fixture preferable to a hook?
interview.answer: Non-automatic fixtures are created lazily when a test or hook requires them. Automatic fixtures run for each test or worker, so they are useful for global per-test or per-worker behavior.
interview.followUp: How can hooks be replaced globally? Declare the before/after behavior in an automatic fixture, using worker scope when it should cover every file in a worker.

keyPoints: Declare an automatic fixture with tuple syntax and the auto option.
Place preparation before await use(), then place cleanup after it.
The runner brackets the consumer with setup and teardown.
Dependencies determine lifecycle order: prerequisites initialize first and clean up last.
Automatic fixtures can express before-each and after-each behavior globally.
gotchas: An automatic fixture runs whether the test lists it or not, so enabling one can add setup and teardown to every applicable test or worker.
A regular fixture is lazy; use automatic scope only when implicit execution is intended.
Scope changes cleanup timing: test scope resets after each test, whereas worker scope lasts until the worker process ends.

Test hooks::globalSetup and globalTeardo.summary: Run Playwright setup once before all tests and cleanup once afterward. Configure separate modules, or return cleanup from setup; project dependencies offer a test-project-based alternative.
Test hooks::globalSetup and globalTeardo.explanation: Set `globalSetup` and `globalTeardown` in Playwright configuration to point to modules that each export a function. Playwright invokes setup once before all tests and teardown once after them; setup can also return the teardown function, and setup data can be exposed through environment variables.

example.title: Configure global setup and teardown
example.explanation: This configuration runs the exported setup function before the test run and the teardown function after it.

useCases.title: Database preparation
useCases.scenario: Create or seed shared test data before browser tests begin.

useCases.title: Shared service startup
useCases.scenario: Launch a service or reserve a port needed by the entire run.

useCases.title: Run-wide cleanup
useCases.scenario: Remove test data and release resources after all tests complete.

interview.question: What does globalSetup do?
interview.answer: `globalSetup` names a module that Playwright loads before the tests. That module must export one function, which Playwright runs once for the test run.
interview.followUp: How can setup values reach tests? Set them on `process.env` in the setup module, then read those environment variables in tests.

interview.question: When does globalTeardown run?
interview.answer: `globalTeardown` points to a module loaded after all tests. Its module must export a single function, which Playwright executes once after the test run.
interview.followUp: Can teardown be colocated with setup? Yes: have the global setup function return the cleanup function.

interview.question: Why might project dependencies be preferable to global hooks?
interview.answer: Project dependencies provide an alternative based on test projects. A setup project runs first, dependent projects run afterward, and a configured teardown project runs after its dependent projects finish.
interview.followUp: What happens with `--no-deps`? Playwright ignores project dependencies and their teardowns, so only directly selected projects run.

keyPoints: Configure `globalSetup` when a resource or service must be prepared once before the complete test run.
Configure `globalTeardown` for one-time cleanup after every test has finished.
The setup module contract is one exported function receiving the configuration object.
Playwright invokes the setup function once, rather than once per test or worker.
Expose values created during setup by assigning them to `process.env`.
The documentation presents standalone global-hook files and project dependencies as the two approaches.
gotchas: Each global setup module must export one function; it receives the configuration object.
Use environment variables to transfer setup-created values such as ports or authentication tokens to tests.
A setup module can return its cleanup function instead of configuring a separate global teardown module.

Test hooks::test.afterEach.summary: `test.afterEach` registers work that runs after every applicable test. Use it to undo per-test setup and inspect the finished result with fixtures and `TestInfo`, including attaching diagnostics.
Test hooks::test.afterEach.explanation: Register an asynchronous callback that Playwright runs after every test in the surrounding file or describe group. The callback receives the same fixtures as the test plus TestInfo, so it can clean up per-test resources and inspect the completed test result or attach diagnostic data.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Optional label shown for the hook; the overload without a title is also supported.

parameters.name: hookFunction
parameters.description: Asynchronous or synchronous callback executed after each applicable test; it receives fixtures and may receive TestInfo.

Test hooks::test.afterEach.returns: The documentation describes hook registration and does not specify a return value.

example.title: Attach diagnostics after an unexpected result
example.explanation: This hook records the page URL as an attachment when the completed test status differs from its expected status.

useCases.title: Per-test teardown
useCases.scenario: A beforeEach hook creates records, files, or other per-test resources that must not affect later tests.

useCases.title: Result-aware diagnostics
useCases.scenario: A test may fail or finish unexpectedly and the failure needs contextual information.

useCases.title: Describe-group cleanup
useCases.scenario: A group of related tests needs common post-test behavior without applying it to the entire file.

interview.question: When does `test.afterEach` run and what is its scope?
interview.answer: `test.afterEach` registers a callback that runs after each test. Declared at file scope, it applies to tests in that file; inside `test.describe`, it applies to tests in that group.
interview.followUp: How can the callback inspect the result? Pass or use `TestInfo`; its status is available after the test has finished, and compare it with `expectedStatus`.

interview.question: What can an after-each callback access?
interview.answer: The callback can use all fixtures available to the test body and receives `TestInfo`. This makes it suitable for both per-test teardown and result-dependent diagnostics such as attachments.
interview.followUp: What should be considered when adding expensive cleanup? Its time is charged against the separate timeout shared by fixture teardowns and afterEach hooks.

interview.question: How would you use the hook for cleanup and diagnostics?
interview.answer: Use `test.afterEach` to tear down resources created in `beforeEach`, such as removing test data. It also supports checking whether the actual status matches the expected status and collecting information when it does not.
interview.followUp: How would you apply a hook to every test globally? Use an auto fixture rather than a file- or group-scoped hook.

keyPoints: The callback runs once after every test covered by the hook.
A file-level declaration covers each test in that test file.
Putting it inside a describe group limits its coverage to tests in that group.
The hook can use the fixtures exposed to the test body, enabling per-test cleanup.
TestInfo supplies metadata and controls useful for result-aware post-test work.
Pair it with beforeEach when each test needs resources removed afterward.

Test hooks::test.beforeAll and afterAll.summary: test.beforeAll and test.afterAll run setup and cleanup once per worker around tests in a file or describe group. Use them to share worker-level resources, while remembering that worker restarts can repeat the lifecycle.
Test hooks::test.beforeAll and afterAll.explanation: Use these hooks for setup and cleanup surrounding all tests in a file or describe group. Each hook runs once per worker, so resources created in beforeAll can be released in afterAll; worker restarts can cause the lifecycle to run again.
Test hooks::test.beforeAll and afterAll.syntax:
test.beforeAll(hookFunction)
test.beforeAll(title, hookFunction)
test.afterAll(hookFunction)
test.afterAll(title, hookFunction)

example.title: Share a page within one worker
example.explanation: A page is created once for the worker before the file's tests and closed after them. The browser fixture remains available for setup, while each test can use the shared page created by the hook.

useCases.title: Worker-level resource lifecycle
useCases.scenario: Create a shared page, browser resource, or service before a group of tests and close it afterward.

useCases.title: API test data management
useCases.scenario: Prepare test data or an API repository before tests and delete it after the group completes.

useCases.title: Reduce repeated setup
useCases.scenario: Avoid repeating expensive setup for every individual test when the resource can safely be shared within a worker.

interview.question: When do beforeAll and afterAll execute?
interview.answer: beforeAll runs once per worker before the tests in its file or describe group, and afterAll runs once per worker afterward. A file-level hook surrounds that file, while a hook inside describe surrounds the group.
interview.followUp: How does parallelism affect shared state? Each worker is independent, so a separate worker can create its own resource and cannot use another worker's in-memory state.

interview.question: How should resources created in beforeAll be cleaned up?
interview.answer: Use beforeAll to create a resource shared by the covered tests and afterAll to release it. The hook callbacks can use fixtures such as browser, allowing a page or external resource to be prepared once per worker.
interview.followUp: What if a test fails? The worker can be discarded and restarted, so setup may run again and cleanup may execute in the replacement worker.

interview.question: What are the available declarations and scopes?
interview.answer: The supported signatures are test.beforeAll(hookFunction) or test.beforeAll(title, hookFunction), with the analogous two forms for afterAll. A hook declared in a describe group is limited to that group.
interview.followUp: How would you run setup once for all files? Define an automatic worker-scoped fixture instead of relying on a file-level hook.

keyPoints: At file scope, the pair brackets every test declared in that file.
Each worker executes the hook lifecycle independently, so multiple workers can perform setup and teardown separately.
A file-level beforeAll completes before the file's tests begin.
Placing beforeAll inside describe limits its setup to the tests in that group.
Pair resource creation in beforeAll with matching disposal in afterAll.
gotchas: A worker restart after a test failure causes afterAll to run again in the replacement worker; do not assume cleanup runs only once for the entire test command.
A hook inside describe applies to that group rather than automatically covering every test in the file.
Other applicable hooks still run after one hook fails, so cleanup should tolerate partial setup.

Test hooks::test.beforeEach.summary: Registers setup that Playwright runs before each test. It can use the same fixtures as the test, including page, and can be scoped to a file or test.describe group.
Test hooks::test.beforeEach.explanation: Call test.beforeEach with an asynchronous function to prepare state before each test. Playwright supplies the fixtures requested by the hook, such as page, and can also provide TestInfo. A hook declared in a file applies to that file's tests; one inside test.describe applies only to tests in that group.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Optional hook title.

parameters.name: hookFunction
parameters.description: Function receiving the requested fixtures and optional TestInfo.

example.title: Navigate before every test
example.explanation: The hook navigates the isolated page before every test, so each test starts from the same URL.

useCases.title: Reset page location
useCases.scenario: Navigate to a starting URL before each test so tests begin from a predictable page.

useCases.title: Arrange isolated test state
useCases.scenario: Create or configure per-test page-object state using the page fixture.

useCases.title: Configure browser behavior
useCases.scenario: Install per-test browser-context routing or initialization before navigation.

interview.question: What does test.beforeEach do, and where does its scope apply?
interview.answer: test.beforeEach registers a hook that runs before every test. At file scope it covers tests in that file; inside test.describe, it covers tests in that group. The hook can request the same fixtures as the test and optionally receive TestInfo.
interview.followUp: How would you apply setup to every test across files? Use an automatic fixture rather than declaring a separate hook in each file.

interview.question: What arguments can a beforeEach hook receive?
interview.answer: The hook function receives a fixtures object, such as { page }, and may receive a second TestInfo argument. Playwright sets up requested fixtures before running the hook, allowing setup such as navigation or state initialization.
interview.followUp: How can the hook adjust the timeout for tests that use it? Accept TestInfo and call testInfo.setTimeout with the desired timeout.

interview.question: How are multiple beforeEach hooks ordered, and how is cleanup handled?
interview.answer: Registering more than one beforeEach hook is supported. Playwright executes those hooks in the order in which they were registered, so their registration order determines setup order.
interview.followUp: What should be used for cleanup of resources created by the hook? Register test.afterEach to tear down resources established by beforeEach.

keyPoints: Use test.beforeEach to run preparation before every test rather than repeating the same setup in each test body.
A file-level hook applies to each test declared in that test file.
Put the hook in test.describe when setup should be limited to that group.
Request fixtures in the hook exactly as in a test, including the page fixture used for per-test browser state.
Accept TestInfo as the second argument when setup needs information about the currently running test.
Pair beforeEach resource setup with afterEach cleanup when the setup creates resources requiring explicit teardown.
gotchas: Do not call test.use inside a beforeEach hook; configure fixture overrides in the file scope or a test.describe group instead.
Multiple hooks are order-dependent, so register setup in the sequence required by later hooks and tests.

Test hooks::test.fail and test.fixme.summary: test.fail() runs a test and verifies that it fails, while test.fixme() prevents a known-broken test from running. Both can be applied declaratively or conditionally with an optional explanation.
Test hooks::test.fail and test.fixme.explanation: Use test.fail() when Playwright should execute a test and verify that it fails. Use test.fixme() when the test is known to need fixing and should not continue running; both can be declared conditionally or inside a test, and descriptions can document the reason.
Test hooks::test.fail and test.fixme.syntax:
test.fail(title, body)
test.fail(title, details, body)
test.fail(condition, description)
test.fail(callback, description)
test.fail()

test.fixme(title, body)
test.fixme(title, details, body)
test.fixme(condition, description)
test.fixme(callback, description)
test.fixme()

parameters.description: Test title when declaring an annotation.

parameters.name: details
parameters.description: Optional test details when declaring an annotation.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: Test body when declaring an annotation.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Condition or callback used for runtime annotation.

parameters.name: description
parameters.description: Optional explanation shown with the annotation.

Test hooks::test.fail and test.fixme.returns: No value; the annotation changes how Playwright schedules and evaluates the test.

useCases.title: Track a known broken behavior
useCases.scenario: A known defect is expected to produce a failing assertion and should remain covered.

useCases.title: Temporarily disable impractical execution
useCases.scenario: A test crashes or takes too long to execute while an issue is unresolved.

useCases.title: Annotate selected configurations
useCases.scenario: Only one browser, device, or environment has the unresolved problem.

interview.question: How does test.fail() behave?
interview.answer: test.fail() runs the test and checks that its result is failing. It is useful for documenting a known broken behavior until the implementation is fixed.
interview.followUp: What happens if the test unexpectedly passes? Playwright reports that expectation as a problem, exposing that the defect may have been fixed.

interview.question: When should test.fixme() be used instead of test.fail()?
interview.answer: test.fixme() marks the test as needing repair and does not run it. This is appropriate when execution is slow or crashes, rather than when a failing test can safely be exercised.
interview.followUp: How can it be configuration-specific? Call test.fixme(condition, description) so only matching configurations are aborted and the reason appears in test reporting.

interview.question: What forms do these annotations support?
interview.answer: Both annotations support declaration with a title and body, or runtime use with a condition or callback. A description can explain the expected failure or the reason a test is temporarily fixed.
interview.followUp: Which form is recommended for expected failures? The documentation recommends declaring them with test.fail(title, body).

keyPoints: Use test.fail() to declare that a test is expected to fail.
Expected failures record a known product defect without putting branching logic in the test body.
Use test.fixme() for a test that is acknowledged as broken and should be repaired.
Fixme is suitable when executing the test is impractical because it is slow or causes a crash.
Apply a conditional annotation when the problem exists only for selected configurations.
gotchas: test.fixme() prevents the test from running, unlike test.fail().
A runtime fixme condition must be placed before actions that should not execute.

Test hooks::test.use for overrides.summary: test.use changes Playwright options or fixtures for a whole test file or a test.describe group. Prefer this scoped declaration for overrides instead of reconfiguring inside hooks.
Test hooks::test.use for overrides.explanation: Call test.use with an options object at file scope or inside test.describe to change Playwright settings for that scope. The call can override options or fixtures, but it must not be placed in beforeEach or beforeAll.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Object containing local test options or fixture overrides.

useCases.scenario: Set a locale, timezone, viewport, or other context option for every test in one file.

useCases.title: Describe-scoped configuration
useCases.scenario: Give one test.describe group different browser-context settings from the surrounding file.

useCases.title: Scoped fixture customization
useCases.scenario: Provide a function-valued fixture override for a selected scope.

interview.question: What does test.use do?
interview.answer: test.use accepts an options object and applies those options to a single test file or a test.describe group. It is useful for changing settings such as the context locale without changing the global configuration.
interview.followUp: Where can it be called? At global file scope or inside test.describe; calling it from beforeEach or beforeAll is invalid.

interview.question: How do file and describe scopes differ?
interview.answer: A file-level call affects tests in that file, while a call inside test.describe limits the setting to that group. This lets a narrower group override the broader file behavior.
interview.followUp: How would you keep the override from affecting another file? Put the call in the file that owns the tests, because test.use is file-local.

interview.question: Can test.use override fixtures as well as options?
interview.answer: The argument is an object of local options, and test.use can also override a fixture by receiving a function. This makes both built-in settings and fixture behavior configurable for the selected scope.
interview.followUp: What should replace a hook-based reconfiguration? Declare the desired option or fixture override with test.use at file or describe scope.

keyPoints: Use test.use to apply options or fixture overrides to one file or one describe group.
A common use is selecting a locale, which configures the test context.
The declaration belongs at file scope or inside test.describe.
Pass an object containing the options intended for that scope.
A function value can replace or customize a fixture for the selected scope.
gotchas: Do not call test.use from beforeEach or beforeAll; configure the scope directly instead.
A test.use override is file-local and does not change tests in other files.
